question: Explain the difference between Dijkstra's algorithm and the Bellman-Ford algorithm for shortest paths.

key_points: Dijkstra's greedily picks the closest unvisited node each step using a priority queue, running in O((V+E) log V) — but requires all edge weights to be non-negative
Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges repeatedly for V-1 iterations, running in O(V*E) — slower, but correctly handles negative edge weights
Bellman-Ford can also detect negative weight cycles (an extra pass checking if any edge can still be relaxed indicates one exists); Dijkstra cannot handle or detect these at all
Choose Dijkstra when weights are guaranteed non-negative for better performance; choose Bellman-Ford when negative weights are possible or cycle detection is needed
reference_solution.sample_answer: Dijkstra's algorithm greedily expands the closest unvisited node at each step, typically implemented with a priority queue, running in O((V+E) log V) time — but it assumes all edge weights are non-negative, since its greedy choice can be wrong if a later negative edge could produce a shorter path. Bellman-Ford instead relaxes every edge repeatedly for V-1 iterations, which is slower at O(V*E), but it correctly handles negative edge weights since it doesn't commit to a node's shortest distance early. Bellman-Ford can also detect negative weight cycles with one extra pass — if any edge can still be relaxed after V-1 iterations, a negative cycle exists — which Dijkstra can't do or handle at all. In practice, I'd use Dijkstra whenever weights are guaranteed non-negative for its better performance, and Bellman-Ford specifically when negative weights are possible or cycle detection matters.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to explain why Dijkstra's greedy approach breaks down in the presence of negative edge weights, with a concrete counterexample.

question: What is dynamic programming, and how do you identify whether a problem can be solved with it?

key_points: DP solves problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and storing (memoizing) their results to avoid redundant recomputation

Two required properties to apply DP: optimal substructure (the optimal solution to a problem can be built from optimal solutions to its subproblems) and overlapping subproblems (the same subproblems recur multiple times during naive recursion)
Two implementation styles: top-down memoization (recursive, cache results as computed) and bottom-up tabulation (iterative, build up a table of results from base cases)
Contrast with divide-and-conquer, whose subproblems typically don't overlap (e.g. merge sort), so memoization wouldn't help there
reference_solution.sample_answer: Dynamic programming solves a problem by breaking it into subproblems, but specifically leverages the fact that those subproblems overlap — the same subproblem gets solved repeatedly in a naive recursive approach — and stores their results so each subproblem is computed only once. To tell if DP applies, I'd look for two properties: optimal substructure, meaning the optimal answer to the whole problem can be constructed from optimal answers to its subproblems, and overlapping subproblems, meaning a plain recursive solution would redundantly recompute the same subproblem many times. You can implement DP either top-down, with recursion plus memoization caching results as you go, or bottom-up, iteratively filling a table starting from base cases. This is different from divide-and-conquer approaches like merge sort, where the subproblems don't actually overlap, so memoization wouldn't provide any benefit there.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to identify the overlapping subproblems in naive recursive Fibonacci and show how memoization fixes the exponential blowup.

question: Explain how a trie (prefix tree) works and give a use case where it outperforms a hash map.

key_points: A trie stores strings character by character down a tree structure, where each node represents a prefix shared by all strings passing through it
Lookup/insert of a string of length L takes O(L) time regardless of how many strings are stored, since you just walk down matching characters
Use case where it beats a hash map: prefix-based queries — 'find all words starting with prefix X' or autocomplete, which a hash map can't do efficiently (it would need to check every key)
Trade-off: tries can use more memory than a hash map due to per-character node overhead, especially with sparse/varied alphabets, unless compressed (e.g. a radix tree)
reference_solution.sample_answer: A trie stores a set of strings by breaking them into individual characters along paths in a tree, where every node represents a prefix shared by all the strings that pass through it — so common prefixes are stored just once instead of duplicated across strings. Both lookup and insertion take O(L) time, where L is the length of the string, since you're just walking down the tree matching one character at a time, and this doesn't depend on how many total strings are stored. Where a trie clearly outperforms a hash map is for prefix-based queries — like autocomplete, or 'find all words starting with a given prefix' — since a hash map has no efficient way to enumerate keys sharing a prefix without scanning every key, while a trie just walks to the prefix's node and explores everything beneath it. The trade-off is a trie can use more memory than a hash map, due to the per-character node overhead, though this can be mitigated with a compressed variant like a radix tree that merges chains of single-child nodes.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to implement autocomplete (returning all words with a given prefix) using a trie.

question: What is the time complexity of building a heap from an unsorted array, and why is it O(n) rather than O(n log n)?

key_points: Naively, you might think inserting n elements one at a time (each O(log n)) gives O(n log n) to build a heap — but the standard 'heapify' bottom-up approach does better
Heapify calls sift-down starting from the last non-leaf node up to the root; most nodes are near the bottom of the tree where sift-down does very little work (a leaf needs 0 sift-down steps)
Summing the work across all levels (a geometric-like series where most nodes do O(1) work and only a few near the root do up to O(log n) work) gives a total of O(n), not O(n log n)
This is a good example of amortized/aggregate analysis producing a better bound than a naive per-operation multiplication would suggest
reference_solution.sample_answer: You might naively assume building a heap takes O(n log n), reasoning that inserting n elements one at a time each costs O(log n). But the standard build-heap algorithm doesn't insert one at a time — it calls sift-down starting from the last non-leaf node up through the root, and here's the key insight: most nodes in a heap are near the bottom of the tree, and a node near the bottom has very little distance to sift down — a leaf node needs zero work, nodes just above leaves need at most one swap, and so on. When you sum the total work across all levels, it forms a series where the vast majority of nodes contribute only O(1) work and just a few nodes near the root contribute up to O(log n), and that sum actually converges to O(n) overall, not O(n log n). It's a classic example of aggregate analysis giving a tighter bound than naively multiplying a per-operation cost by the number of operations.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to at least sketch the summation showing why the total work converges to O(n).

question: Explain the union-find (disjoint set) data structure and how path compression and union by rank improve its performance.

key_points: Union-find tracks a collection of disjoint sets, supporting 'find' (which set does an element belong to) and 'union' (merge two sets), commonly used for connectivity/cycle-detection problems like Kruskal's MST algorithm
Naive implementation: find/union can degrade to O(n) per operation if the tree structure becomes a long chain
Union by rank/size: always attach the smaller/shallower tree under the root of the larger/deeper one during union, keeping trees shallow

Path compression: during find, make every node on the path point directly to the root, flattening the structure for future lookups — combined, these give near-constant (inverse Ackermann function) amortized time per operation
reference_solution.sample_answer: Union-find maintains a collection of disjoint sets and supports two operations: find, which tells you which set/representative an element belongs to, and union, which merges two sets together — it's commonly used for connectivity problems, like detecting cycles when building a minimum spanning tree with Kruskal's algorithm. A naive implementation, where union just attaches one tree's root under another's arbitrarily, can degrade into a long chain, making find take O(n) in the worst case. Union by rank (or size) fixes this by always attaching the smaller or shallower tree under the root of the larger one during a union, keeping the overall tree shallow. Path compression further optimizes find by making every node visited along the way point directly to the root once it's found, flattening the structure so future lookups on those nodes are nearly instant. Combined, these two optimizations bring the amortized time per operation down to nearly O(1) — technically O(inverse Ackermann function of n), which is effectively constant for any realistic input size.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to implement union-find with both path compression and union by rank from scratch.
